notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for 1 John 5, drawn from the sources I was able to search and read:

---

## 1 John 5 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — "Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father also loves those born of Him."

- **Faith as the evidence of regeneration:** John states that believing Jesus is the Christ is how one is "born of God"—not a mere intellectual assent but a trusting, reliant faith. This counters any idea that love earns salvation; we are born of God by trusting Jesus and His saving work. (enduringword.com)
- **Gill** adds: this is not a bare profession but "a believing with the heart unto righteousness… a looking to, and trusting in the righteousness of Christ for justification." True faith is "the evidence of regeneration." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-john-5.html)
- **Love for the family:** Being born of God has two effects: love for the Father who begot us, and love for all who are begotten of Him. This common birth—not race, class, denomination, or politics—is the ground of Christian fellowship. (enduringword.com)
- **Ellicott** notes: genuine faith in Christ is the genuine birth from God. From that faith, through that birth, comes proper family love—"sympathy with real Christians." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_john/5.htm)
- **Cambridge Bible:** Faith that does not lead to love, and love that is not based on faith, "must come to nothing." (biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/1_john/5.htm)

---

### v. 2 — "By this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and keep His commandments."

- **The test of genuine love for the brethren:** True love for God's children is shown by loving God and keeping His commandments. Love for the brethren springs from love to God, not from natural affection, social bonds, or self-interest. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-john-5.html, enduringword.com)
- **Ellicott:** If we doubt the quality of our love, we ask ourselves whether we are loving God and keeping His commandments—"the true work of faith." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_john/5.htm)
- **Guzik:** The best thing a father can do for his children is to love his wife—so too, the first way to love brothers and sisters in Christ is to love and obey God. (enduringword.com)

---

### v. 3 — "For this is the love of God, that we keep His commandments. And His commandments are not burdensome."

- **Love = obedience:** Loving God is not a "mushy emotional experience" (Boice, cited by Guzik). It shows itself in keeping His commandments, echoing Jesus' words: "If you love Me, keep My commandments" (John 14:15). (enduringword.com)
- **Not burdensome, for four reasons:** (1) God's commands are gifts—like a "manufacturer's handbook" for the best life; (2) the new birth gives new hearts that want to obey (Jeremiah 31:33); (3) compared with the Pharisees' hundreds of rules, Jesus' yoke is easy and light (Matthew 11:30); (4) love makes obedience a joy—"Love feels no loads." (enduringword.com)
- **Gill:** The commands in view are especially "those of faith in Christ, and love to the saints" (1 John 3:23), plus Gospel ordinances. They are not heavy to regenerate persons. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-john-5.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** The world makes God's commands seem grievous, but the new birth gives an unworldly nature and strength that conquers the world. (biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/1_john/5.htm)

---

### v. 4 — "because everyone born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith."

- **The principle:** If we are born of God, we will overcome the world. It was unthinkable to John that anything born of God could be defeated by this world. (enduringword.com)
- **Cambridge Bible:** The neuter "whatsoever" (Greek) emphasizes the victorious power, not the person: "It is not the man, but his birth from God, which conquers." (biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/1_john/5.htm)
- **Gill:** "The world" includes Satan, the lusts of the world, false prophets, and wicked men who would turn believers from obeying God. Faith—centered on Christ the object, not the grace itself—overcomes all. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-john-5.html)
- **Faith is the instrument of victory:** Not a one-time saving faith only, but a "consistently abiding faith"—ongoing reliance and trust upon Jesus Christ. (enduringword.com)
- **Precept Austin:** "Overcomes" is present tense—born-again ones are "continually overcoming" the fallen world. The victory is Christ's; believers share in it. (preceptaustin.org/1_john_55_commentary)

---

### v. 5 — "Who then overcomes the world? Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God."

- **Believing Jesus is the Son of God:** This means He is the eternal God, the second Person of the Trinity in human flesh—not merely a man with a "Christ-spirit." (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org/1_john_55_commentary, citing Steven Cole)
- **Spurgeon (cited by Guzik):** The word "believe" does not merely mean intellectual assent, but "to trust, to confide in, to commit to, entrust with" — "the very marrow of the meaning of faith is confidence in, reliance upon." (enduringword.com)
- **Gill:** The victory is not owing to faith itself but to its object Christ, who has overcome the world and makes believers "more than conquerors." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-john-5.html)
- **Bookends:** John begins with "believes that Jesus is the Christ" (v.1) and ends with "believes that Jesus is the Son of God" (v.5); love, obedience, and victory all flow from Christ. (preceptaustin.org/1_john_55_commentary)

---

### v. 6 — "This is the One who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ—not by water alone, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies to this, because the Spirit is the truth."

- **"The most perplexing passage in the Epistle"** (Plummer, cited by Boice). Four main interpretations have been offered:
  1. **Baptism and Crucifixion** (Tertullian, oldest view): "Water" = Jesus' baptism (identifying with sinful humanity); "blood" = His crucifixion (standing in our place). John insists Jesus was Son of God at both His baptism *and* His death—countering the heresy that the "Christ Spirit" left Jesus before the cross. (enduringword.com)
  2. **The sacraments** (Luther, Calvin): Water = baptism, blood = communion. Jesus comes to us through the two sacraments. (enduringword.com)
  3. **The piercing of Jesus' side** (Augustine): The water and blood flowing from Jesus' side at the cross (John 19:34). (enduringword.com)
  4. **Natural birth and death**: Water of the womb, blood of death—emphasising Jesus' genuine humanity against Gnostic "phantom" ideas. (enduringword.com)
- **Ellicott:** Water = Christ's baptism, symbolising fulfilment of the Law in perfect purity; blood = His meritorious cross and passion; the Spirit = demonstrable proofs of His kingdom. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_john/5.htm)
- **The Spirit bears witness:** The Holy Spirit testifies to the true person of Jesus (John 15:26; 16:14). His consistent message is "Here is Jesus." (enduringword.com)

---

### vv. 7–8 — "For there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood—and these three are in agreement."

**The Johannine Comma (text-critical issue):**

- The KJV/NKJV include an expanded reading: "For there are three that bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness on earth…" **These words do not appear in any Greek manuscript until the 14th century.** They appear only in the Latin Vulgate. (enduringword.com)
- **No early Church Father** ever quoted the expanded words during the Trinitarian debates of the first centuries—though they quoted vv. 6 and 8. (enduringword.com)
- **Erasmus** reluctantly added them in 1522 after being challenged, on the basis of a suspect manuscript (Codex Montfortii) he believed was fabricated. This became part of the Textus Receptus and thus the KJV. (enduringword.com)
- The BSB follows the earliest reading, omitting the added Trinitarian formula. (biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_john/5.htm)
- **Gill** (writing in the 18th century as a Baptist) defended the longer reading as genuine, citing its presence in some Latin manuscripts, Cyprian (3rd century), and arguing it was omitted by "unfaithful interpreters." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-john-5.html)
- **The three witnesses:** Spirit, water, and blood "agree as one"—they all testify consistently to who Jesus is. His life, death, and the Spirit tell one unified story. (enduringword.com)
- **JFB:** The Spirit is an additional witness besides water and blood, attested at Jesus' baptism by descending on Him, throughout His ministry, and permanently in the Church through the New Testament and in believers' hearts. (biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/1_john/5.htm)

---

### v. 9 — "Even if we accept human testimony, the testimony of God is greater. For this is the testimony that God has given about His Son."

- **Ellicott:** "Any message that clearly comes from God is to be accepted by us with a readiness infinitely greater than in the case of mere human testimony." The threefold witness from God conveys a certainty no human evidence could claim. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_john/5.htm)
- **The argument from lesser to greater:** If we accept human testimony in daily life (in courts, etc.), how much more should we receive God's testimony about His Son? (enduringword.com)

---

### v. 10 — "Whoever believes in the Son of God has this testimony within him; whoever does not believe God has made Him out to be a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has given about His Son."

- **Internal witness:** The believer has the testimony "within him"—the inner witness of the Holy Spirit confirming the truth about Jesus. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_john/5.htm)
- **The gravity of unbelief:** To reject God's testimony about His Son is to call God a liar—a stark and sobering statement. Faith honours God; unbelief impugns His character. (enduringword.com)

---

### v. 11 — "And this is that testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son."

- **The content of God's testimony:** God has granted eternal life, and it resides exclusively in His Son. (enduringword.com)
- **Ellicott:** "The Christian creed is here reduced to a very small compass: the gift of eternal life and the dependence of that life upon His Son." Eternal life is not mere endless existence, but "that life in God, thought of without reference to time, which can have no end… Its opposite is not annihilation, but the second death: existence in exclusion from God." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_john/5.htm)

---

### v. 12 — "Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life."

- **Exclusive and absolute:** "Having the Son" is His dwelling in the heart by faith—a conscious reality that transforms life's whole character. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_john/5.htm)
- There is no eternal life apart from a living relationship with Jesus Christ. This parallels John 3:36. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_john/5.htm)

---

### v. 13 — "I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life."

- **Purpose of the letter:** John writes so believers may *know* they have eternal life—assurance rests on God's promise, not on fluctuating feelings. This echoes John 20:31. (biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_john/5.htm; enduringword.com)
- **Ellicott:** John sums up his object: that they "may feel certain that the eternal life which ought to be theirs is theirs already, and that their belief may not cease, but may be really vital." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_john/5.htm)

---

### v. 14 — "And this is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us."

- **Confidence in prayer:** Assurance of eternal life fuels bold, confident prayer. The condition is "according to His will"—prayer aligned with God's character and revealed will. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_john/5.htm)
- **Praying according to God's will** means praying in alignment with His promises in Scripture, His character, and His purposes. When we pray this way, "we work with Him as partners, aligning our will with His." (enduringword.com)

---

### v. 15 — "And if we know that He hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we already possess what we have asked of Him."

- **Assurance of answer:** If we know God hears (because we prayed according to His will), we can be confident the petition is granted—even if the visible answer is not yet seen. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_john/5.htm)

---

### vv. 16–17 — "If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death… There is a sin that leads to death; I am not saying he should ask regarding that sin. All unrighteousness is sin, yet there is sin that does not lead to death."

**This is one of the most debated passages in the epistle. Several major views exist:**

#### View 1: The "sin unto death" is final rejection of Christ by an unbeliever (spiritual/eternal death).

- **John MacArthur (GTY):** The sin leading to death may be that of a non-Christian leading to eternal death—a final, persistent rejection of Jesus Christ, such as the blasphemy of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 12:31–32). Prayer for such people is not forbidden, but John says it will not be answered; God has already made the final decision. The present tense "sinning" (Greek) often describes habitual sins that characterise unbelievers in 1 John (3:4, 6, 8; 5:18). (shop.gty.org/library/bibleqnas-library/QA0131/the-sin-unto-death, from search excerpt)
- **Monergism.com (Reformed):** The person in v.16b "is no more a believer than the brother of verse 16a." He is most likely one of the false teachers, a counterfeit Christian exposed by his departure (1 John 2:19). The sin unto death is the blasphemy of the Holy Spirit—"deliberate and persistent rejection of Jesus Christ." Believers cannot commit this sin because, by definition, it is the sin that makes one an unbeliever. (monergism.com/blog/intercession-and-apostasy-1-john-516-17, from search excerpt)

#### View 2: The "sin unto death" is a believer's sin so serious that God takes that person's physical life.

- **MacArthur (alternative view):** God may discipline a sinning believer with physical death (e.g., Ananias and Sapphira in Acts 5:1–11; the Corinthians who abused the Lord's Table in 1 Corinthians 11:30). The sin is not one particular sin, but any sin the Lord determines warrants such severe chastisement. (shop.gty.org/library/bibleqnas-library/QA0131/the-sin-unto-death, from search excerpt)

#### View 3 (Piper/Desiring God): The "sin not leading to death" is any sin we can still authentically confess and repent from.

- **John Piper:** The sin that does not lead to death (eternal death/damnation) is "any sin that we commit that we are, by grace, capable of truly confessing and repenting from." John is striking a balance: Christians do sin, and not all sin leads to damnation. The "sin unto death" is the unforgivable sin—a sin that puts one beyond repentance. When John says "I am not saying he should ask regarding that sin," he means "that's not what I'm talking about"—not a prohibition on prayer. (desiringgod.org/interviews/what-is-the-sin-not-leading-to-death-in-1-john-5, from search excerpt)

#### View 4 (The Gospel Coalition summary):

- TGC identifies four views: (1) a believer commits both sins and the second apostatises (incorrect); (2) an unbeliever commits both sins (less likely); (3) a believer commits both sins, and God may discipline with physical death (more likely); (4) a believer commits sin not to death, an unbeliever commits sin to death (most likely). (thegospelcoalition.org/essay/sin-unto-death, from search excerpt)

**On v. 17:** "All unrighteousness is sin, yet there is sin that does not lead to death"—John affirms that not every sin is fatal to the soul. Christians do sin, but not all sin leads to eternal death. This guards against perfectionism. (desiringgod.org, from search excerpt)

---

### v. 18 — "We know that anyone born of God does not keep on sinning; the One who was born of God protects him, and the evil one cannot touch him."

- **"Does not keep on sinning":** The present tense indicates a continuous, habitual practice of sin—not sinless perfection. The one born of God is not characterised by a lifestyle of sin. (enduringword.com)
- **"The One who was born of God"** = Jesus Christ. He protects (or "keeps") the believer. The Greek verb for "touch" means "to lay hold of" or "cling to"—Satan cannot attach himself to or seize the believer. (enduringword.com)
- **Gill:** Believers "through the use of the armour of God, and the power of divine grace… keep themselves from the evil one, and he cannot come at them, to draw them into this sin [the sin unto death]." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-john-5.html)

---

### v. 19 — "We know that we are of God, and that the whole world is under the power of the evil one."

- **Two families, two destinies:** Believers belong to God; the world system lies in the power of the evil one. This sharp antithesis runs throughout 1 John. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_john/5.htm)
- **"Under the power"** (Greek: "lies in"): The world is under Satan's sway, contrasted with the believer's security in Christ. (enduringword.com)

---

### v. 20 — "And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding… He is the true God and eternal life."

- **Christ gives understanding:** Jesus has given believers spiritual discernment to know "Him who is true" (God the Father). Believers are "in Him who is true"—in God through union with His Son. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_john/5.htm)
- **"He is the true God and eternal life":** A debated reference. The nearest antecedent is "His Son Jesus Christ"—making this a direct declaration of Christ's deity. Some argue the antecedent is "Him who is true" (the Father). Most traditional commentators see this as referring to Jesus Christ. (enduringword.com)
- **Ellicott:** "The God of whom the Son had spoken was that true God, and to know Him as such in His Son was eternal life." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_john/5.htm)

---

### v. 21 — "Little children, keep yourselves from idols."

- **Abrupt but fitting ending:** After declaring Jesus as the true God and eternal life, John warns against anything that might claim allegiance apart from Him. Idols include not only literal pagan images but subtle ones: career, wealth, appearance, relationships, or anything that competes with God for devotion. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_john/5.htm)
- **Gill:** As believers keep themselves from Satan, they must also "keep themselves from idols of all sorts." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-john-5.html)
- This is John's final word: only a real relationship with the true God sustains us; idols must be utterly rejected. (enduringword.com)

---

## Summary of Key Points Where Traditions Differ

| Issue | Positions |
|---|---|
| **The Johannine Comma (vv. 7–8)** | Modern evangelical scholarship (enduringword.com, biblehub.com) and nearly all modern translations view the Trinitarian addition as a late scribal insertion. **Gill** (older Baptist) defended it as genuine. **King James Only** advocates defend its inclusion. The **Catholic** Vulgate includes it. |
| **"Water and blood" (v. 6)** | **Tertullian/Enduring Word:** Baptism and crucifixion. **Luther and Calvin:** The sacraments (baptism and Lord's Supper). **Augustine:** The piercing of Jesus' side (John 19:34). |
| **"Sin unto death" (vv. 16–17)** | **Baptist/Reformed (MacArthur, Monergism):** Often the sin of an unbeliever (final rejection of Christ) or a believer's sin leading to physical death. **Piper (Baptist/Reformed):** Any sin from which one cannot repent; the unforgivable sin. **Arminian/Wesleyan** commentators (e.g., I. Howard Marshall) may see it as apostasy by a true believer. |
| **"He is the true God" (v. 20)** | Most **evangelical** commentators see a direct assertion of Christ's deity. Some **Unitarian** and modern critical scholars argue the antecedent is the Father, not the Son. |
